generics.comment: A generic argument list `<T, U>` is a bracketed construct, not a run of comparison operators, and the `>>` that closes a nested one is two brackets rather than a right shift. Both are matched as begin/end regions so the closing `>` is consumed one at a time, which is the only way `table<table<integer>>` stops highlighting as a shift. Every window is line-local (`[ \t]`, and an `$` alternative on each `end`) so an unclosed `<` colours one line rather than running away to the end of the file.

patterns.comment: The same list on a declaration `fn name<T, U>(...)`, where the name defines a function rather than calling one. Listed first so it beats the call form below. Anchored with a lookbehind because `#keywords` has already consumed the `fn`, so a rule that started there would never get the chance to run — which is what made the old `fn name` rule dead.

Generic call `f<T>(...)`. The trailing `(` is what distinguishes this from `a < b`: the lookahead requires the whole `<...>` window to be type-shaped and to be followed by a call's open paren. One level of nesting is allowed, which covers `filter<table<integer>>(xs)`. The genuinely ambiguous `a < b, c > (d)` still matches — the real parser resolves that by speculative parse (`Parser::try_eat_generic_call_args`), which a regex grammar cannot do.

`table<V>` / `table<K, V>` in a type position. Anchored on `table` alone because it is the one generic head that cannot be a variable being compared — `table` is a primitive type name, so `table <` is never a less-than. User-written generic types (`Box<T>`) are deliberately not anchored here: generics are still accept-and-discard in the parser, and `Name <` is ambiguous.

generic-body.comment: What may appear between the angle brackets. `#generics` first so a nested list opens its own region and eats its own `>`; `#types` supplies the primitive and PascalCase names without a second copy of the primitive list.

patterns.comment: PascalCase identifiers treated as type/class names
patterns.name: entity.name.type.saule

patterns.comment: The name in a declaration `fn name(...)`. Anchored on the name with a lookbehind rather than on the `fn`: `#keywords` is included earlier and wins the tie at the `fn`, so a rule matching from there never fires. Listed ahead of the call rule below so a declaration is not mistaken for a call.
Compound assignment first, so `..=` is one token rather than `..` plus a stray `=`, and `<<=` / `>>=` beat both the shifts and `<=` / `>=`.
patterns.name: keyword.operator.assignment.saule

patterns.comment: Before the comparison rule: otherwise `<<` matches `<` and a shift highlights as two comparisons. `<=` / `>=` cannot match here, so nothing is stolen the other way.
patterns.name: keyword.operator.bitwise.saule
